plĭco (plĭcāvi, plĭcui, acc. to Prisc. p. 680 P.), plĭcātum and plĭcĭtum, āre, v. a. root plic-; Gr. πλέκω; v. plecto,
I.to fold, to lay or wind together, to fold up, double up (poet. and in post-class. prose; cf.: “complico, plecto, necto, flecto),” Lucr. 4, 828 : “quaedam plicata,” id. 6, 1086 : “chartam,” Mart. 4, 83, 7 : seque in sua membra plicantem (anguem), winding or coiling himself up, Verg. A. 5, 279; Gell. 17, 9, 9: decas plena his quattuor numeris gradatim plicatis integratur, folded
together, i. e. added, Mart. Cap. 7, § 734: “ostiola plicabantur,” Vulg. Ezech. 41, 24 : “et cum plicuisset librum,” id. Luc. 4, 20 .
From A Latin Dictionary (Charlton T. Lewis, Charles Short, Oxford, Clarendon Press, 1879)
